actions.justification: Mandatory action — assess HR, BP, SpO2, RR for hemodynamic stability and to classify PE severity (massive vs submassive).
Mandatory action — Wells criteria risk stratification is essential for determining pre-test probability of PE in a patient with pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea.
Mandatory action — D-dimer is a key diagnostic step in PE workup; elevated levels combined with Wells score guide further imaging (CTPA).

AHA Class I recommendation: 12-lead ECG should be obtained within 10 minutes for acute chest pain. At 15 minutes, this is overdue. ECG will help evaluate for STEMI, right heart strain (S1Q3T3 pattern suggestive of PE), and arrhythmias. Critical in this patient with suspected PE.

Patient presents with acute dyspnea. Although SpO2 is 98%, supplemental oxygen is appropriate supportive care during the assessment phase of suspected pulmonary embolism to maintain adequate oxygenation reserve.

Chest X-ray is indicated in the initial assessment of acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain to evaluate for alternative diagnoses (pneumothorax, pneumonia, pleural effusion) and complement the PE workup. Per AHA guidelines, chest X-ray should be obtained as soon as possible.

Echocardiogram helps assess right heart strain, which would support diagnosis of pulmonary embolism and guide risk stratification. Patient has HIT comorbidity which significantly impacts anticoagulation choice, so accurate diagnosis is critical before treatment.

CT pulmonary angiography is the gold standard for diagnosing pulmonary embolism. Given this patient's presentation (acute dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain) and elevated Wells score, CT-PA is urgently indicated to confirm PE diagnosis before initiating alternative anticoagulation (avoiding heparin/LMWH due to HIT comorbidity).

Given the complexity of this case - suspected PE in a patient with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia requiring non-heparin anticoagulation (e.g., argatroban or fondaparinux) - pulmonology consultation is warranted to assist with management decisions and anticoagulation strategy.

A 12-lead ECG is recommended per AHA guidelines within 10 minutes of presentation for acute chest pain to evaluate for STEMI/ST changes. Although an ECG was previously ordered (order_ecg), order_imaging_ecg is a distinct available action ID and should be completed to ensure formal ECG acquisition and interpretation given pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea.

This patient has acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain with a history of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, raising high suspicion for pulmonary embolism. Lower extremity Doppler ultrasound to evaluate for DVT is a standard component of PE workup and supports diagnosis while CT-PA results are pending.

Echocardiogram is indicated to assess for right heart strain, which would support massive or submassive PE diagnosis and guide risk stratification and management decisions, especially relevant given the HIT comorbidity which limits anticoagulation choices.
ABG will assess oxygenation status, A-a gradient, and ventilatory adequacy, which helps stratify PE severity and guides treatment decisions.
BNP is a prognostic marker in PE, reflecting right ventricular strain. Elevated BNP would indicate higher-risk PE and influence management decisions.
BMP provides baseline metabolic and renal function data, essential before initiating anticoagulation (especially important given HIT history requiring non-heparin alternatives).
Patient has known HIT — CBC with platelet count is critical to assess current thrombocytopenia severity and guide safe anticoagulation selection for suspected PE.
Baseline coagulation studies (PT/INR/aPTT) are needed before initiating anticoagulation therapy and to assess coagulation status in a patient with HIT and suspected PE.
Serum lactate assesses tissue perfusion and helps risk-stratify the PE (massive vs. submassive), which will guide urgency and type of treatment despite currently stable hemodynamics.

Troponin is indicated per AHA chest pain guidelines for risk stratification in acute chest pain/dyspnea with suspected PE. It also helps assess right heart strain from PE. This has not yet been ordered.

Patient has suspected PE (acute dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain) with CT-PA ordered. Given the critical comorbidity of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT), standard heparin and LMWH are contraindicated. 'give_anticoagulation' likely represents a non-heparin alternative (e.g., argatroban, fondaparinux, or rivaroxaban) appropriate for HIT patients with suspected PE.

Patient has confirmed HIT, making heparin and LMWH contraindicated. With suspected/confirmed PE, interventional radiology should be consulted for potential catheter-directed therapy or mechanical thrombectomy as alternative to systemic anticoagulation with heparin-based agents.

Supportive IV fluid administration for a patient with suspected PE can help maintain preload and right ventricular filling pressure. Patient is currently hemodynamically stable but monitoring and fluid support are appropriate while definitive PE management is being arranged.

Patient has HIT (heparin-induced thrombocytopenia) as a comorbidity, making heparin and LMWH contraindicated. Thrombolysis is not indicated given hemodynamic stability (BP 120/80, HR 80, SpO2 98%). Vasopressor monitoring/readiness is appropriate as a precautionary supportive measure given suspected PE in the context of HIT where standard anticoagulation options are limited.

Patient has heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT), making heparin and LMWH contraindicated. With acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain suggesting pulmonary embolism, and given the HIT comorbidity, thrombolysis may be indicated if imaging confirms massive PE. This is the safest available anticoagulation/treatment option from the list given the HIT contraindication to heparin-based therapies.
